screens.title: ROS Parameters and the Parameter Server
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore the Parameter Server, the central configuration store ROS provides so nodes can share settings at runtime. You will learn what kinds of values it holds, how to set and read them from the command line, how to load YAML parameter sets, and how Python and C++ nodes access those values. This matters because hardcoding configuration forces rebuilds and makes experiments slow; parameters let you change behavior across simulation and real robot deployments quickly and consistently. We will look at concrete examples: setting a robot name and sensor frequency with the rosparam tool, storing PID gains in a nested YAML map, and reading those values from a Python node using get_param with defaults. You will also see how private parameters prevent naming conflicts when multiple node instances run. By the end you should be able to create a YAML file for a robot, load it into the Parameter Server, and write nodes that read and optionally write parameters at runtime. Consider which robot settings you would make configurable in your next experiment.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › ROS Parameters

ROS Parameters and the Parameter Server

Use a shared dictionary to store typed configuration: strings, numbers, booleans, lists and maps. Parameters let you adapt nodes at runtime and switch between simulation and real hardware without recompiling.

In this lesson
Set and get params, write YAML files, and read values from Python and C++ nodes.
Why it matters
Avoid recompiles and centralize configuration for reproducible experiments.
Coming up
Hands-on: create robot_config.yaml, load it and read values in nodes.
Visual concept
Parameter Server
Shared key-value store
Typed values, named like file paths, e.g. /robot_name, /pid_gains/kp
Multiple access methods
Command line, YAML files, Python and C++ APIs
Example
A YAML file defines pid_gains as nested keys; nodes read them using get_param or nh.param and use defaults when missing.
Explore Key Topics
rosparam CLI
Set, get, list, dump and load parameters.
YAML files
Store nested configs, lists and maps for different deployments.
Node APIs
Read with defaults and validate values at runtime.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives guide our work with the Parameter Server. First, you will be able to store and retrieve configuration values using the rosparam tools and the Parameter Server APIs. That reduces the need to rebuild nodes when you change settings. Second, you'll learn three ways to set parameters: directly from the command line, programmatically from nodes, and by loading YAML files. This makes it easy to swap configurations between simulation and hardware. Third, you will understand the difference between private, node, and global parameters, including using the tilde prefix to create per-node parameters and the leading slash for global values that all nodes can access. Fourth, you'll practice using dynamic parameter types: strings, integers, floats, booleans, lists and nested dictionaries, and you'll learn to validate values after reading them. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and an action step so you can verify competency when you complete the hands-on activity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Validation
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives frame the hands-on work. You will create a YAML configuration for a simulated robot and load it into the Parameter Server, demonstrating that values are available to nodes without recompilation. You'll implement a Python node that reads parameters with sensible default values and logs them, showing how get_param works and why defaults prevent crashes when a key is missing. You'll also build a C++ node that uses nh. param to fetch typed values and prints them, verifying parity between language APIs. Finally, you'll practice modifying a YAML file and reloading parameters to observe runtime updates. Throughout, validate values after reading them; for example, ensure a sensor frequency is positive. This step helps you avoid common runtime failures and makes your system robust under different deployments. In practical terms, skills you'll demonstrate in the hands-on activity. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: What is the Parameter Server?
screens.narratorSegment: The Parameter Server is a central, in-memory dictionary that ros core creates when you start roscore. It stores named, typed values and makes them available to every node on the ROS network. When we say typed, we mean basic types like integer, float, boolean and string, plus structured types such as lists and dictionaries. Parameters are addressed with names that look like file paths, for example /robot_name or /pid_gains/kp. Using a central store keeps configuration separate from code. That separation matters in practice: you can tune controller gains, change sensor frequencies, or point to a different map file without rebuilding nodes. A common misconception is that parameters are persistent across system restarts: by default they live in memory while roscore runs. If you need persistent sets, you save them to YAML and reload on startup. Another practical point is that the Parameter Server is not a replacement for a full database; it is intended for configuration and small-sized structured data. As you design your system, ask which values truly need to be runtime-configurable, and keep ephemeral or heavy telemetry out of parameters. Reflect: which of your robot's values belong in the Parameter Server and which do not?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is the Parameter Server?
Core definition

A shared, typed key-value store available to all nodes while roscore is running. Names resemble filesystem paths and values support strings, numbers, booleans, lists and maps.

Analogy
Think of the Parameter Server as a filing cabinet: drawers are namespaces and each card is a parameter you can put in or take out with rosparam or a node API.
Common misconception
Parameters persist only while roscore runs unless you save them to YAML; they are not a database for telemetry.
Key takeaway
Use parameters for configuration, not for high-volume or persistent data.
Examples of parameter names
  • /robot_name
  • /sensor_frequency
  • /robot1/pid_gains/kp
Why this matters
Centralized config simplifies experiments and deployments. A single YAML file can define all parameters for simulation or hardware, keeping behavior reproducible and auditable.

screens.title: Parameter Namespaces and Naming
screens.narratorSegment: Parameter names form a hierarchical namespace, similar to file paths. A leading slash denotes a global name that lives at the root, for example /robot_name. Node-specific or private parameters use a tilde prefix, for example ~max_speed inside a node named motor_controller becomes /motor_controller/max_speed when resolved. You can also create nested parameters using path separators to group related values, for example /pid_gains/kp or /robot1/pid_gains/kp. Nested structures are particularly useful for controller gains or grouped configuration sets. A useful rule is: use global parameters for system-wide settings like simulation_mode or robot_name, and use private parameters for per-node tuning like max_speed or publish_rate when multiple instances run. A common mistake is relying on relative names without understanding the node's namespace, which can lead to unexpected conflicts or missing values. Always document the parameter names you expect and consider prefixing node names in launch files so private parameters resolve predictably. Ask yourself: if I run two instances of the same node, will their parameters collide? If yes, make them private. Parameter Namespaces and Naming means use prefixes to control scope: leading / for global, ~ for node-private, and / separators for nested groupings.. In practical terms, global names, private names, and nested keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Namespaces & Naming
Hierarchy view
Parameters use path-like names. Example namespaces:
/robot_name
/simulation_mode
/pid_gains/kp
/robot1/pid_gains/kp
Private parameter example
Inside a node named motor_controller, the name ~max_speed resolves to /motor_controller/max_speed at runtime.
Guidelines
  • Global (/) for system-wide values like robot_name or simulation_mode.
  • Private (~) for node-local tuning to avoid conflicts when multiple instances run.
  • Use nested keys to group related values such as pid_gains or sensor settings.
Check your understanding
If you run two motor_controller nodes, how will you give each its own max_speed? Answer: use private parameters or unique node namespaces.

screens.title: rosparam CLI: set, get, list, dump, load, delete
screens.narratorSegment: The rosparam command-line tool is indispensable for quick experiments. With rosparam set you can add or change a parameter on the running Parameter Server. For example, rosparam set /robot_name "my_robot" stores the robot name immediately. rosparam get retrieves a parameter value for verification, and rosparam list shows all parameter names currently present. To remove a parameter use rosparam delete. If you want to save the whole server state to disk, rosparam dump writes a YAML snapshot you can version and reuse. rosparam load reads a YAML file and writes those keys into the server. Use case: while testing a controller, increase sensor_frequency with rosparam set and observe system behavior without restarting nodes. A common misconception is that rosparam load replaces only new keys; in fact it will write the keys in the file into the server — existing keys with the same names will be overwritten. Always verify after load with rosparam get or rosparam list. These commands let you iterate quickly on configuration during development and debugging. rosparam CLI: set, get, list, dump, load, delete means use rosparam set/get/list/delete for quick edits, and dump/load to move parameter sets between disk and memory.. In practical terms, command-line control for rapid experiments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › rosparam CLI
Common rosparam commands
# Set a parameter
rosparam set /robot_name "my_robot"
rosparam set /sensor_frequency 40
rosparam set /simulation_mode false

# Get a parameter
rosparam get /robot_name

# List all parameters
rosparam list

# Delete a parameter
rosparam delete /robot_name

# Dump all parameters to YAML
rosparam dump params.yaml

# Load parameters from YAML
rosparam load params.yaml
Practical tips
  • After loading a YAML, verify important keys with rosparam get to ensure types are correct.
  • Use dump to snapshot working configurations before experiments.
  • Remember that load will overwrite existing keys with the same names.
Example scenario
During tuning, change sensor_frequency and observe behavior. If the value breaks the system, restore from a saved YAML snapshot.

screens.title: YAML Parameter Files
screens.narratorSegment: YAML is the standard format for ROS parameter files because it expresses nested maps and lists in a readable way. A typical configuration groups related values under logical keys. For example, pid_gains contains nested kp, ki and kd keys, while waypoints is a list of coordinate pairs. The YAML structure maps directly to Parameter Server keys: pid_gains: kp: 2.0 creates /pid_gains/kp in the server when loaded. Lists become arrays that nodes can read as Python lists or C++ vectors. A concrete YAML example from the lesson declares robot_name, simulation_mode, sensor_frequency, pid_gains and waypoints. When using YAML, be careful with types: unquoted numbers are numeric, and booleans are true/false. A common mistake is forgetting indentation or using tabs; YAML is indentation-sensitive. Also validate that lists have the intended structure — waypoints as a list of two-element lists is different than a list of dictionaries. After loading a YAML file, always confirm key existence and type in your node before using the value in control logic. YAML Parameter Files means yaml maps to parameter server names and types; nested maps become nested keys and lists become arrays.. In practical terms, structure, lists, and nested dictionaries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › YAML Parameter Files
Example YAML
robot_name: "turtlebot_01"
simulation_mode: false
sensor_frequency: 40

pid_gains:
  kp: 2.0
  ki: 0.1
  kd: 0.5

waypoints:
  - [0.0, 0.0]
  - [1.0, 2.0]
  - [3.0, 1.0]
Best practices
  • Keep separate YAML files per deployment (simulation vs real robot).
  • Document expected types and ranges for each parameter.
  • Use clear names and nested groups for related settings.
Validation tip
After loading a YAML, test a few values in your node and check types to catch accidental string/number mismatches.

screens.title: Reading and Setting Parameters in Python
screens.narratorSegment: Python's rospy A P I makes working with parameters straightforward. Use rospy. get_param with a key and an optional default to read a value safely. For example, get_param('/robot_name', 'default_robot') returns either the stored name or the provided default when the key is missing. Use rospy. set_param to write values at runtime. The lesson includes a small Python node pattern: initialize the node, read parameters including nested keys like /pid_gains/kp with defaults, log the values, and set a status parameter. This pattern shows two important habits: supply defaults to avoid exceptions and validate values after reading them — for instance check that sensor frequency is positive. If you're polling parameters for live updates, make sure to avoid tight loops and consider sleeping or using timers. A common misconception is thinking set_param automatically notifies all nodes; it only changes the stored value; nodes must read the parameter to see updates. To get live behavior, a node should re-read parameters at appropriate times or subscribe to a custom topic that signals a reload. In short: use get_param with defaults, validate, and plan how and when your node rereads parameters.

keyIdea.text: Use rospy.get_param with defaults and rospy.set_param to read and update parameters, validating values after reading them.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Python: get_param & set_param
Example Python node
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy

if __name__ == '__main__':
  rospy.init_node('param_reader')

  # Get parameters with default values
  robot_name = rospy.get_param('/robot_name', 'default_robot')
  sensor_freq = rospy.get_param('/sensor_frequency', 10)
  simulation = rospy.get_param('/simulation_mode', True)

  # Nested parameter
  kp = rospy.get_param('/pid_gains/kp', 1.0)

  rospy.loginfo("Robot: %s, Freq: %d Hz, Sim: %s, Kp: %.2f",
                robot_name, sensor_freq, simulation, kp)

  # Set a parameter
  rospy.set_param('/status', 'running')
Practical notes
  • Always use defaults when a missing key would cause an error.
  • Validate numeric ranges after reading values.
  • Use set_param to signal state changes, but readers must poll or be notified to react.
Check your code
Will your node handle a missing /pid_gains key? Use defaults and validation to avoid crashes.

screens.title: Accessing Parameters from C++
screens.narratorSegment: C++ nodes use the NodeHandle APIs to read and write parameters. The templated nh. param method reads a parameter into a typed C++ variable and accepts a default value. For example, nh. param ("/robot_name", robot_name, "default_robot") ensures that robot_name has a sensible fallback. For numeric and boolean types, nh. param, nh. param, and nh. param are common. To set a parameter you use nh. setParam with the key and value. The C++ example in the lesson demonstrates reading robot name, sensor frequency, simulation flag, and a nested kp value, then logging them and setting a /status parameter. A practical difference from Python is type handling and conversions in C++; you must ensure your default types match the stored type to avoid surprises. Also remember to include the appropriate headers and initialize ros::init and NodeHandle before calling nh. param. As with Python, validate values after fetching them — for example confirm sensor_freq is positive — and document the expected parameter names and types in your package README so other developers know what to provide. Accessing Parameters from C++ means use nh.param<t> with defaults to read typed parameters and nh.setparam to write them from c++ nodes.. In practical terms, nh.param and nh.setparam patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Example C++ node
#include <ros/ros.h>

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
  ros::init(argc, argv, "param_reader");
  ros::NodeHandle nh;

  std::string robot_name;
  int sensor_freq;
  bool simulation;
  double kp;

  nh.param("/robot_name", robot_name, "default_robot");
  nh.param("/sensor_frequency", sensor_freq, 10);
  nh.param("/simulation_mode", simulation, true);
  nh.param("/pid_gains/kp", kp, 1.0);

  ROS_INFO("Robot: %s, Freq: %d, Sim: %d, Kp: %.2f",
           robot_name.c_str(), sensor_freq, simulation, kp);

  nh.setParam("/status", "running");

  return 0;
}

screens.title: Private vs Global Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Private parameters live under a node's namespace and are declared with a tilde. For example, within a node named motor_controller, asking for ~max_speed resolves to /motor_controller/max_speed in the global namespace. Global parameters start with a slash and are shared by all nodes. Use global parameters for system-wide settings such as robot_name or simulation_mode that every node should know. Use private parameters when different instances of the same node need their own tuning values, such as per-motor max_speed values for left and right controllers. A typical error is assigning what should be a private tuning value as a global parameter and then running multiple node instances, which causes both instances to read and write the same key and produce conflicts. Another subtle point: launch files can remap namespaces, so private parameters still resolve under the node's effective namespace. When designing systems, choose the least-privileged scope necessary to avoid accidental interference. Ask: does this value need to be shared by many nodes, or is it specific to one instance? That question guides your choice. Private vs Global Parameters means use ~ for per-node settings to avoid clashes, and / for system-wide configuration accessible to all nodes.. In practical terms, when to use ~ versus / and why it prevents conflicts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Global parameters
Start with a leading slash. Shared by all nodes. Example: /robot_name, /simulation_mode.
Private parameters
Precede with a tilde inside a node. Example: ~max_speed resolves to /<node_name>/max_speed. Useful for per-node tuning.
Side-by-side example
If two motor_controller nodes run as /left_motor and /right_motor, each can use ~max_speed to have /left_motor/max_speed and /right_motor/max_speed, preventing conflicts that would occur if a single global /max_speed were used.
Misconception
Private parameters are not magically isolated from remapping; namespaces and launch file remaps affect resolution, so be explicit in launch configurations.

screens.title: Setting Parameters from Nodes and Reloading
screens.narratorSegment: Nodes can both read and write parameters. In Python use rospy. set_param and in C++ nh. setParam. Writing parameters is handy for reporting state, enabling features, or saving computed configuration. For larger config changes, modify your YAML file and use rosparam load to push the new values into the Parameter Server. If nodes need to act on updated values, they must re-read the parameters at appropriate times. A straightforward approach is to check parameters periodically in a loop or timer callback and apply changes when values differ. Another pattern is to implement a parameter reload service or a small topic that signals nodes to refresh their configuration. A common trap is assuming setParam pushes changes to nodes automatically. It doesn't: setParam updates server state, and only reading nodes will see the changes. If your node caches parameter values, make sure to plan when it will refresh them. For safety-critical settings, consider gating live updates behind validation logic so a bad YAML edit doesn't drive unsafe behavior. When reloading YAML files in experiments, use rosparam dump beforehand so you can restore a known-good state if needed.

screens.title: Parameter Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Good parameter hygiene makes systems easier to run and safer to change. First, organize parameters into YAML files per deployment environment — for example simulation_params. yaml and real_robot_params. yaml — so you can load the right set quickly. Second, document each parameter's purpose, type and valid range in README or package documentation so users and future you know what to supply. Third, always validate parameter values immediately after reading them: confirm numeric ranges, non-empty strings for file paths, and correct list sizes for structured inputs like waypoints. Another recommended practice is to use private parameters for node-specific tuning to avoid collisions when running multiple instances, and reserve global parameters for settings that truly apply system-wide. Version-control your YAML files and use rosparam dump to create snapshots before experiments. Finally, prefer small, focused parameters for critical settings rather than burying many values in a single large structure; clarity helps prevent dangerous misconfigurations. These habits reduce confusion, speed up experiments, and prevent runtime surprises. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting Tips
screens.narratorSegment: Several common errors recur when working with parameters. First, missing keys: if your code assumes a parameter exists and doesn't provide a default, it may crash or behave unpredictably. Always use get_param or nh. param with a default. Second, wrong types: YAML parsing creates typed values; if you expect an integer but the YAML contains a quoted string, your node may misinterpret it. Validate types after reading and coerce only when safe. Third, namespace confusion: private parameters resolve under node namespaces and launch-file remaps can change that resolution. If a key seems missing, confirm the resolved name using rosparam list and check the full path. Other tips: use rosparam dump to snapshot working states before experiments, use small tests to check that nested keys like /pid_gains/kp exist, and prefer explicit parameter names in launch files to reduce surprises. If runtime updates don't appear in a node, ensure that node actually re-reads the parameter rather than relying on an initial cached copy. These habits make debugging faster and experiments safer. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore the Parameter Server, the central configuration store ROS provides so nodes can share settings at runtime. You will learn what kinds of values it holds, how to set and read them from the command line, how to load YAML parameter sets, and how Python and C++ nodes access those values. This matters because hardcoding configuration forces rebuilds and makes experiments slow; parameters let you change behavior across simulation and real robot deployments quickly and consistently. We will look at concrete examples: setting a robot name and sensor frequency with the rosparam tool, storing PID gains in a nested YAML map, and reading those values from a Python node using get_param with defaults. You will also see how private parameters prevent naming conflicts when multiple node instances run. By the end you should be able to create a YAML file for a robot, load it into the Parameter Server, and write nodes that read and optionally write parameters at runtime. Consider which robot settings you would make configurable in your next experiment.

These four objectives guide our work with the Parameter Server. First, you will be able to store and retrieve configuration values using the rosparam tools and the Parameter Server APIs. That reduces the need to rebuild nodes when you change settings. Second, you'll learn three ways to set parameters: directly from the command line, programmatically from nodes, and by loading YAML files. This makes it easy to swap configurations between simulation and hardware. Third, you will understand the difference between private, node, and global parameters, including using the tilde prefix to create per-node parameters and the leading slash for global values that all nodes can access. Fourth, you'll practice using dynamic parameter types: strings, integers, floats, booleans, lists and nested dictionaries, and you'll learn to validate values after reading them. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and an action step so you can verify competency when you complete the hands-on activity.

These objectives frame the hands-on work. You will create a YAML configuration for a simulated robot and load it into the Parameter Server, demonstrating that values are available to nodes without recompilation. You'll implement a Python node that reads parameters with sensible default values and logs them, showing how get_param works and why defaults prevent crashes when a key is missing. You'll also build a C++ node that uses nh. param to fetch typed values and prints them, verifying parity between language APIs. Finally, you'll practice modifying a YAML file and reloading parameters to observe runtime updates. Throughout, validate values after reading them; for example, ensure a sensor frequency is positive. This step helps you avoid common runtime failures and makes your system robust under different deployments. Learning Objectives — Practice & Validation means create yaml, load parameters, read them in python and c++, and verify runtime updates and validation.. In practical terms, skills you'll demonstrate in the hands-on activity. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Parameter Server is a central, in-memory dictionary that ros core creates when you start roscore. It stores named, typed values and makes them available to every node on the ROS network. When we say typed, we mean basic types like integer, float, boolean and string, plus structured types such as lists and dictionaries. Parameters are addressed with names that look like file paths, for example /robot_name or /pid_gains/kp. Using a central store keeps configuration separate from code. That separation matters in practice: you can tune controller gains, change sensor frequencies, or point to a different map file without rebuilding nodes. A common misconception is that parameters are persistent across system restarts: by default they live in memory while roscore runs. If you need persistent sets, you save them to YAML and reload on startup. Another practical point is that the Parameter Server is not a replacement for a full database; it is intended for configuration and small-sized structured data. As you design your system, ask which values truly need to be runtime-configurable, and keep ephemeral or heavy telemetry out of parameters. Reflect: which of your robot's values belong in the Parameter Server and which do not?

Parameter names form a hierarchical namespace, similar to file paths. A leading slash denotes a global name that lives at the root, for example /robot_name. Node-specific or private parameters use a tilde prefix, for example ~max_speed inside a node named motor_controller becomes /motor_controller/max_speed when resolved. You can also create nested parameters using path separators to group related values, for example /pid_gains/kp or /robot1/pid_gains/kp. Nested structures are particularly useful for controller gains or grouped configuration sets. A useful rule is: use global parameters for system-wide settings like simulation_mode or robot_name, and use private parameters for per-node tuning like max_speed or publish_rate when multiple instances run. A common mistake is relying on relative names without understanding the node's namespace, which can lead to unexpected conflicts or missing values. Always document the parameter names you expect and consider prefixing node names in launch files so private parameters resolve predictably. Ask yourself: if I run two instances of the same node, will their parameters collide? If yes, make them private. Parameter Namespaces and Naming means use prefixes to control scope: leading / for global, ~ for node-private, and / separators for nested groupings.. In practical terms, global names, private names, and nested keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The rosparam command-line tool is indispensable for quick experiments. With rosparam set you can add or change a parameter on the running Parameter Server. For example, rosparam set /robot_name "my_robot" stores the robot name immediately. rosparam get retrieves a parameter value for verification, and rosparam list shows all parameter names currently present. To remove a parameter use rosparam delete. If you want to save the whole server state to disk, rosparam dump writes a YAML snapshot you can version and reuse. rosparam load reads a YAML file and writes those keys into the server. Use case: while testing a controller, increase sensor_frequency with rosparam set and observe system behavior without restarting nodes. A common misconception is that rosparam load replaces only new keys; in fact it will write the keys in the file into the server — existing keys with the same names will be overwritten. Always verify after load with rosparam get or rosparam list. YAML is the standard format for ROS parameter files because it expresses nested maps and lists in a readable way. A typical configuration groups related values under logical keys. For example, pid_gains contains nested kp, ki and kd keys, while waypoints is a list of coordinate pairs. The YAML structure maps directly to Parameter Server keys: pid_gains: kp: 2.0 creates /pid_gains/kp in the server when loaded. Lists become arrays that nodes can read as Python lists or C++ vectors. A concrete YAML example from the lesson declares robot_name, simulation_mode, sensor_frequency, pid_gains and waypoints. When using YAML, be careful with types: unquoted numbers are numeric, and booleans are true/false. A common mistake is forgetting indentation or using tabs; YAML is indentation-sensitive. Also validate that lists have the intended structure — waypoints as a list of two-element lists is different than a list of dictionaries. After loading a YAML file, always confirm key existence and type in your node before using the value in control logic. Python's rospy A P I makes working with parameters straightforward. Use rospy. get_param with a key and an optional default to read a value safely. For example, get_param('/robot_name', 'default_robot') returns either the stored name or the provided default when the key is missing. Use rospy. set_param to write values at runtime. The lesson includes a small Python node pattern: initialize the node, read parameters including nested keys like /pid_gains/kp with defaults, log the values, and set a status parameter. This pattern shows two important habits: supply defaults to avoid exceptions and validate values after reading them — for instance check that sensor frequency is positive. If you're polling parameters for live updates, make sure to avoid tight loops and consider sleeping or using timers. A common misconception is thinking set_param automatically notifies all nodes; it only changes the stored value; nodes must read the parameter to see updates. To get live behavior, a node should re-read parameters at appropriate times or subscribe to a custom topic that signals a reload. In short: use get_param with defaults, validate, and plan how and when your node rereads parameters.

C++ nodes use the NodeHandle APIs to read and write parameters. The templated nh. param method reads a parameter into a typed C++ variable and accepts a default value. For example, nh. param ("/robot_name", robot_name, "default_robot") ensures that robot_name has a sensible fallback. For numeric and boolean types, nh. param, nh. param, and nh. param are common. To set a parameter you use nh. setParam with the key and value. The C++ example in the lesson demonstrates reading robot name, sensor frequency, simulation flag, and a nested kp value, then logging them and setting a /status parameter. A practical difference from Python is type handling and conversions in C++; you must ensure your default types match the stored type to avoid surprises. Private parameters live under a node's namespace and are declared with a tilde. For example, within a node named motor_controller, asking for ~max_speed resolves to /motor_controller/max_speed in the global namespace. Global parameters start with a slash and are shared by all nodes. Use global parameters for system-wide settings such as robot_name or simulation_mode that every node should know. Use private parameters when different instances of the same node need their own tuning values, such as per-motor max_speed values for left and right controllers. A typical error is assigning what should be a private tuning value as a global parameter and then running multiple node instances, which causes both instances to read and write the same key and produce conflicts. Another subtle point: launch files can remap namespaces, so private parameters still resolve under the node's effective namespace. When designing systems, choose the least-privileged scope necessary to avoid accidental interference. Ask: does this value need to be shared by many nodes, or is it specific to one instance? Nodes can both read and write parameters. In Python use rospy. set_param and in C++ nh. setParam. Writing parameters is handy for reporting state, enabling features, or saving computed configuration. For larger config changes, modify your YAML file and use rosparam load to push the new values into the Parameter Server. If nodes need to act on updated values, they must re-read the parameters at appropriate times. A straightforward approach is to check parameters periodically in a loop or timer callback and apply changes when values differ. Another pattern is to implement a parameter reload service or a small topic that signals nodes to refresh their configuration. A common trap is assuming setParam pushes changes to nodes automatically. It doesn't: setParam updates server state, and only reading nodes will see the changes. If your node caches parameter values, make sure to plan when it will refresh them. For safety-critical settings, consider gating live updates behind validation logic so a bad YAML edit doesn't drive unsafe behavior. When reloading YAML files in experiments, use rosparam dump beforehand so you can restore a known-good state if needed.

Good parameter hygiene makes systems easier to run and safer to change. First, organize parameters into YAML files per deployment environment — for example simulation_params. yaml and real_robot_params. yaml — so you can load the right set quickly. Second, document each parameter's purpose, type and valid range in README or package documentation so users and future you know what to supply. Third, always validate parameter values immediately after reading them: confirm numeric ranges, non-empty strings for file paths, and correct list sizes for structured inputs like waypoints. Another recommended practice is to use private parameters for node-specific tuning to avoid collisions when running multiple instances, and reserve global parameters for settings that truly apply system-wide. Version-control your YAML files and use rosparam dump to create snapshots before experiments. Finally, prefer small, focused parameters for critical settings rather than burying many values in a single large structure; clarity helps prevent dangerous misconfigurations. These habits reduce confusion, speed up experiments, and prevent runtime surprises. Several common errors recur when working with parameters. First, missing keys: if your code assumes a parameter exists and doesn't provide a default, it may crash or behave unpredictably. Always use get_param or nh. param with a default. Second, wrong types: YAML parsing creates typed values; if you expect an integer but the YAML contains a quoted string, your node may misinterpret it. Validate types after reading and coerce only when safe. Third, namespace confusion: private parameters resolve under node namespaces and launch-file remaps can change that resolution. If a key seems missing, confirm the resolved name using rosparam list and check the full path. Other tips: use rosparam dump to snapshot working states before experiments, use small tests to check that nested keys like /pid_gains/kp exist, and prefer explicit parameter names in launch files to reduce surprises. If runtime updates don't appear in a node, ensure that node actually re-reads the parameter rather than relying on an initial cached copy. These habits make debugging faster and experiments safer.
